hook.text: A design starts by naming the things your data is about. So take one sentence. Customers place orders for products.

nouns.text: Circle the nouns... customers, orders, products. Each one's a candidate entity, a kind of thing worth tracking.

many.text: Here's a test. Can there be many of these? Lots of customers, orders, products.

status.text: An order's status, though? That just describes an order. It's a fact, not a thing.

type.text: Now, an entity is a TYPE of thing. The type becomes a table, and each real one, a row.

ada.text: Customers is the table. Ada is one row, because she's one real customer.

apart.text: Products get their own table. A product has a price... and a customer doesn't.

attrs-in.text: So what do you need to remember about each one?

attributes.text: Those facts are attributes. An order has a status, a total, and the date it was placed. Each becomes a column.

domain.text: And every column has a domain, the values it's allowed to hold.

loose.text: Say status is just text. Then anything goes in. Sent, shipped, ship in capitals, done... which ones mean the same?

narrow.text: So narrow it. Four statuses, and no total below zero. Of those four spellings, only shipped gets in.

banana.text: And the status banana? Refused, with the name of the rule it broke.

claims.text: But every rule like that is a claim. Cap a name at twenty characters, and you're claiming no name is longer. Johann Sebastian Bach is twenty-one.

control.text: So be strict about what you control, like statuses. Go easy on what the world sends you, like names.

atomic.text: Keep one value per cell, too. Pack two phone numbers into one, and searching for either finds nothing.

entity-or.text: And a fact with details of its own, or lots of copies, like saved addresses? That's an entity too.

erd-in.text: Boxes and facts. Time to draw them.

chen.text: In nineteen seventy-six, Peter Chen proposed the entity-relationship model: say what the data means before deciding how to store it.

pieces.text: An entity-relationship diagram has three pieces. Boxes are entities, the facts inside are attributes, and lines are relationships.

keys.text: PK marks a primary key, and FK a foreign key.

line.text: Now read the line. One customer places zero or many orders, and each order belongs to exactly one customer.

next.text: But look how much that one line said. Entities never live alone... the lines between them carry as much meaning as the boxes.
